title: The Office Door
dateline: House Baroque. The day after the final trial.
mood: A paper with two red words on it, a bench outside a half-open door, and a whole day of waiting.

hero.alt: A white city curves around a wide blue harbor, seen from high above, a beam of light rising from its tallest tower.

segs.t: Guinevere had the paper out before Hester’s car had pulled away from the Academy gate.
It was a rest day. At the trial she had asked Hester to bring the car at first light.
She had unfolded the paper so often in the night that the fold had gone soft.
Top score,
said the red ink at the bottom.
“Father, I took the top score,” she told the window.
Hester drove, in her gray coat.
“Too fast.” Guinevere sat up straight. “Father. I took the top score.”
“Yes, miss.”
“Was that better?”
“It was the same, miss.”
The medal lay in her lap on its ribbon. Guinevere pinned it to her jacket, then unpinned it.
“Medal or no medal, Hester?”
“Medal, miss.”
She pinned it back on.
She had practiced his answer too, half the night.
Well done, Guinevere.
She tried to hear it now in his voice. His voice would only say what it said through his office door: sit up, again, tomorrow, accounts.
So she said it to herself in her own voice. That would do until he said it himself.
She pulled off one glove. Her knuckles were pink and shiny, split and healed and split again.
All year his only answer had been a board meeting and an empty seat.
Paper is what he reads,
she thought.
He’ll read this.
She meant to leave it on his desk, for him to keep.
The House came into view on its hill above the city. He had said she would be home within the year. She was coming home, as he had said. With this.
Hester followed her up the main stair and stopped at the chair where the long hall began.

Morning filled the tall windows down one side of the hall. Her mother’s portrait hung at the far end. Her father’s office door stood half open. Through the gap Guinevere could see the corner of a desk and a dark sleeve with a fur cuff.

media.alt: The dark outline of a tall man in a fur-collared greatcoat with wide cuffs, one hand a fist, the other holding an open scroll.

segs.t: She sat on the bench across from the door, where she had once done her sums. Her feet reached the floor now. She smoothed the paper on her knee and retied both red bows, though neither had slipped.
A servant came with tea. “The master knows you are here, miss.”
“Thank you.”
He knows,
she thought.
He’ll call me when he’s done.
Under the lamp, beside the sleeve, lay a sheet with the same crest as the one on her knee. Of course. The House was a patron. The Academy had sent him the report, and it had come before she did.
He’s reading it.
She sat up straighter.
The sleeve turned a page.
Morning passed. The tea went cold. Men with ledgers went in by the side door of the office and came out again. Somebody in there laughed once. The half-open door stayed as it was.
At noon Hester spoke from the end of the hall. “You should eat, miss.”
“After.”
Hester stayed on her feet beside the empty chair.
The servant took the cold pot away and brought a fresh one.
“Has Father eaten?” Guinevere asked.
“The master took his lunch at his desk, miss.”
“Good. He forgets.”
That pot went cold too.
In the afternoon her hand rose toward the door to knock. It stopped short of the wood.
If I knock, I’m asking,
she thought.
If he comes out, he means it.
She put the hand back on the paper.

A square of sun from the tall windows crawled across the marble. It reached her shoes, climbed the bench and the wall behind her, and slid along it toward the end of the hall. For a while it lit her mother’s portrait. Then it was gone.
He’ll come out,
she thought.
He’ll see.
At dusk a servant lit the lamps one by one, all the way down to the portrait. In the office the desk lamp was already burning.
All right,
she thought.
I’ll ask.
Guinevere stood.
A lady’s refinement. Three seconds.
She pulled her shoulders back. She held the paper up in both hands, where the gap would show it to him.
“Father. I took the top score.”
It came out right. Not too fast.
When I was small, his hand came out for my sums,
she thought.
It’ll come out for this.
The sleeve did not move.
She kept her face ready. She had practiced that too, the face for
Well done.
Her father’s voice came through the gap, short and cold.
“Stop being so stubborn and focus more on the family business!”
A chair scraped. A door opened and shut somewhere behind the desk. When she looked again, the lamp in there was off.
The gap was dark now. She could not see the desk, or the report on it.
The paper was up in both her hands. She lowered it. Her shoulders stayed back, and she did not know how to put them down.
One. Two. Three.
The three seconds were over. She was still standing there.
He’s had it since last night,
she thought.
He read it. And he stayed in there.
At the far end of the hall, the lamp under her mother’s portrait burned on.
She folded the paper along its soft fold and put it back inside her jacket, under the medal. It was not going on his desk.
Footsteps crossed the marble. Hester had come past the chair. She stopped one step away and did not touch her.
“Miss.”
“Take me to the Academy.”
In the car neither of them spoke. Guinevere kept one hand flat on her jacket, over the fold.
Selrick Academy. That night.
The training hall was dark. Guinevere threw her jacket on the bench by the door and lit the one lamp over the heavy bag. She pulled off her gloves. She did not change, and she did not tape her hands.
Elbow in. Hip first. Hands home after every punch.
The bag jumped on its chain. The old splits on her knuckles opened on the third punch. She kept going until there was red on the canvas.
She called her two drones. Tonight her power was low. Their rings dimmed, and they sank toward the floor.
“Up,” she told them.
They rose. They sank.
“Again.”
It was his word. She said it again anyway.
A whole year,
she thought.
It meant nothing to him.
Fine. I’ll train even harder, until I can’t stand. They’ll all have to see. Even him.
The drones’ rings stayed dim. She held them at her shoulders anyway.
Vexana was in the gallery above the door again. Tonight she stopped with her staff half raised.
The heiress had come in late, and not in uniform. She wore good clothes and her two red bows, and she had not taped her hands.
Vexana had run the same trial yesterday. She had seen this girl win it.
Now there was blood on the canvas, and the girl did not stop. Her drones sagged. Her voice came flat across the hall, telling them again.
Vexana looked at her own white gloves. Under the cloth her palms were ridged and hard. A wooden drill pole had done that, in a yard at dawn, until her hands bled.
She took one step down the gallery stair, toward the lamp.
Stay back.
She stopped on the step. She stood there until the girl sent the drones away and went back to the bag, her back to the door.

Then Vexana went down the rest of the way without a sound. From her pocket she took a roll of cloth tape, the kind she wound around her staff’s grip. She set it on the jacket the girl had thrown on the bench, beside a medal on a ribbon.
The girl under the lamp did not turn around. Vexana went out into the dark. Behind her the bag kept jumping on its chain.
